files.model.yaml:
dsl: 2
model: sellers_tco
title: The seller's TCO
currency: USD

description: >-
  A TCO built by the seller of a system, not by its buyer. The seller cannot see the customer's
  workload or its bill, so the model starts from the customer's spend per host and scales it
  three ways: by how many hosts the customer runs, by the share of that spend that moves with
  the number of hosts, and by the product's benchmark advantage, discounted for how much of it
  carries over to this customer's work. It is top down and linear in hosts. It has no measured
  constant and no ceiling, so it is a definitional model: what a seller can honestly build
  before a customer opens their books (ch23).

nodes:
  # -- the customer, as the seller has to guess them -------------------------------------------------

  horizon:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: year
    value: 5
    label: horizon
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "The web service model's horizon (ch02), the refresh cycle the fleet is bought
        against"
    range: [3, 8]

  usage_hosts:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: host
    label: hosts the customer runs today
    value: 50
    note: >-
      One number: a count, which the customer can give the seller by asking. The chapter's answer
      about customer size is the break-even usage below, and a band here would only blur it.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        The seller's picture of a customer in its market, not a count of any one customer's
        hosts. The customer can replace it with a count, and then it is the customer's figure,
        not the seller's.
    range: [5, 300]

  current_cost_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/host/year
    label: customer's spend per host-year, everything in
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 5000, p90: 11000}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        What the seller supposes a customer spends a year for each host it runs, staff included:
        the whole bill divided by the hosts. Lognormal, because a spend cannot be zero or less and
        its high side runs further than its low. The customer knows this figure; the seller
        does not.
    range: [2000, 20000]

  scaling_share:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: share of the spend that moves with hosts
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.3, likely: 0.5, maximum: 0.8}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        How much of that spend goes away when a host does. Hardware, power, licences and support
        move with the host count; staff and anything bought per site largely do not. A brochure
        that scales the whole bill has set this to one without saying so. Triangular, because it
        is a lowest, most likely and highest guess, and a share has hard ends.
    range: [0.1, 1]

  # -- the product, as the seller describes it -------------------------------------------------------

  benchmark_advantage:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 4
    label: benchmark advantage per host
    note: >-
      One number: the vendor publishes one figure, and a range here would put words in its
      mouth. The doubt about it lives in the transfer factor.
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: >-
        The seller's own benchmark: how much more work one proposed host did than one of the
        customer's current hosts, on the benchmark's workload. Here it is the ratio of the two
        hosts' cores in ch22 (sixty-four against sixteen), standing in for a published result.
    range: [1, 10]

  transfer_factor:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: share of the benchmark advantage that carries over
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 0.4, likely: 0.75, maximum: 1.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: >-
        How much of the benchmark's advantage survives on this customer's work rather than on the
        benchmark's. Nobody has measured it for any customer: that would take running the
        customer's own workload on both hosts. One means the benchmark is the customer's workload.
        Triangular, because it is a lowest, most likely and highest guess, and a seller who
        claimed a more precise shape would be inventing it.
    range: [0.2, 1.2]

  proposed_cost_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/host/year
    value: 12747.123866259795
    label: proposed spend per host-year, staff and move excluded
    note: >-
      One number: the seller's own price, which it states as one figure.
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: >-
        The seller's price for running one proposed host for a year: the host spread over the
        horizon, its licence, support and power, and no staff. Here it is the challenger's quote
        in ch22, worked out per host-year; tests/the_sellers_tco and bench/run_seller.py check
        it against the stamped result.
    range: [5000, 30000]

  move_cost:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD
    value: 250000
    label: cost of the move
    note: >-
      One number: ch22's estimate of the move, held as ch22 holds it, so the two chapters
      price the same move.
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "The challenger's migration cost in ch22: the one-off cost of moving to the
        proposed system"
    range: [50000, 1000000]

  # -- the arithmetic ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

  effective_advantage:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: advantage on the customer's work
    formula: benchmark_advantage * transfer_factor

  proposed_hosts:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: proposed hosts, capacity-equivalent
    note: >-
      Not rounded up. A top-down model counts capacity, not boxes, and rounding here would make
      the break-evens approximate instead of exact.
    formula: usage_hosts / effective_advantage

  current_total:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    label: customer's spend over the horizon, as it is
    formula: usage_hosts * current_cost_per_host * horizon

  proposed_total:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    label: customer's spend over the horizon, with the product
    formula: current_total * (1 - scaling_share) + proposed_hosts * proposed_cost_per_host * horizon + move_cost

  saving:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD
    label: saving over the horizon
    formula: current_total - proposed_total

  margin_per_host_year:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/host/year
    label: saving per current host-year, before the move
    note: >-
      What each host the customer runs today saves a year, before the move is paid for. If it
      is zero or less, no amount of usage pays for the move.
    formula: current_cost_per_host * scaling_share - proposed_cost_per_host / effective_advantage

  current_per_year:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    label: customer's spend a year, as it is
    formula: usage_hosts * current_cost_per_host

  proposed_per_year:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    label: customer's spend a year, with the product
    formula: current_per_year * (1 - scaling_share) + proposed_hosts * proposed_cost_per_host

  saving_per_year:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/year
    label: saving a year, before the move
    formula: current_per_year - proposed_per_year

  payback:
    kind: derived
    unit: year
    label: years until the move is paid back
    note: >-
      A break-even in time: the year in which the savings add up to the cost of the move. Only
      a payback while the saving a year is positive; otherwise the move is never paid back, and
      the figure is negative.
    formula: move_cost / saving_per_year

  break_even_transfer:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: transfer factor at which the saving is zero
    note: >-
      A break-even only while the part of the spend that scales is larger than the cost of the
      move. Below that no transfer factor pays, and the figure is negative.
    formula: usage_hosts * proposed_cost_per_host * horizon / (benchmark_advantage * (current_total * scaling_share - move_cost))

  break_even_usage:
    kind: derived
    unit: host
    label: hosts at which the saving is zero
    note: >-
      A break-even only while the margin per host-year is positive. Otherwise no usage pays, and
      the figure is negative.
    formula: move_cost / (horizon * margin_per_host_year)

outputs:
  - saving
  - current_total
  - proposed_total
  - proposed_hosts
  - margin_per_host_year
  - break_even_transfer
  - break_even_usage
  - saving_per_year
  - payback
files.scenarios/brochure.yaml:
scenario: brochure
title: The brochure
because: >-
  The same model with the two assumptions a brochure makes without writing them down: the
  benchmark carries over whole, and every dollar the customer spends moves with the host count.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides:
  transfer_factor: 1
  scaling_share: 1
files.scenarios/ch22_customer.yaml:
scenario: ch22_customer
title: The seller's model, on ch22's customer
because: >-
  The two figures a seller can learn by asking, pinned to ch22's incumbent: the hosts it runs and
  what it spends per host-year, everything in, at the point estimates. The share that scales and
  the transfer factor stay the seller's guesses, so the result can be set beside ch22's bottom-up
  comparison of the same customer.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides:
  usage_hosts: 54
  current_cost_per_host: 7415.122854685757
files.scenarios/reference.yaml:
scenario: reference
title: The seller's honest model
because: >-
  Every guess about the customer is left as the seller's, and the benchmark is discounted
  by a transfer factor nobody has measured. Every figure the book quotes for this model comes
  from here unless it says otherwise.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides: {}
